findings.title: Blocked email lookup is case-sensitive, allowing trivial bypass
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block?(email) queries `BlockedEmail.where(email: email)` with the exact string passed in, but email addresses elsewhere in the app are normalized (e.g. UsersController#change_email uses Email.downcase, and users may sign up with mixed case). A blocked address stored as 'bad@spam.com' will not match a signup using 'Bad@Spam.com', so the block list can be bypassed simply by varying case. The lookup (and the unique index/uniqueness validation) should compare downcased emails.

findings.title: should_block? performs a DB write inside model validation
findings.body: BlockedEmail.should_block? is invoked from EmailValidator.validate_each, i.e. from within ActiveRecord validation of a User. It increments match_count and calls record.save on the BlockedEmail row as a side effect of validating another model. This means every failed signup attempt (including repeated retries of the same form) triggers a write, the increment is a read-modify-write race under concurrency (lost updates on match_count/last_match_at), and if the BlockedEmail save fails (e.g. stale record) the method silently continues. Statistics tracking should be done outside the validation path, or via an atomic UPDATE (update_counters / SQL increment).

findings.title: Blocked-email check applied to existing users changing email, with no admin path to manage block list
findings.body: The email:true validation runs whenever email_changed? on any User, so an existing (possibly long-standing) member whose address appears in the blocked_emails table can no longer save any change that touches email, and their email changes are rejected with a generic 'is not allowed' message. There is also no admin interface, seed, or API anywhere in this PR that ever creates BlockedEmail records, so the block list cannot be populated and the feature (and its match_count statistics) is effectively dead code as shipped.

findings.title: rejectedEmails comparison is case-sensitive against server-echoed value
findings.body: On a failed signup, the email echoed back in result.values.email is pushed into rejectedEmails, and emailValidation checks `rejectedEmails.contains(email)` with an exact string comparison. If the user retypes the same address with different casing or surrounding whitespace, the client-side rejection is skipped and the form is resubmitted to the server, which rejects it again — the user gets no inline feedback explaining the email is blocked. Normalizing both sides (trim/lowercase) before comparing would make the client check reliable.

findings.title: Blocked email is reported to user as 'invalid'
findings.body: When a signup fails because the email is on the server's block list, the client shows I18n.t('user.email.invalid'), i.e. a malformed-address message, rather than a message explaining the address is not permitted (the server has user.email.blocked for this). The user is told their syntactically valid email is invalid, which is confusing and wrong.

findings.title: Failed-signup response echoes submitted name/username/email back to the client
findings.body: The create failure path now returns `values: user.attributes.slice("name", "username", "email")` to any anonymous requester. Combined with the CSRF skip on create (`skip_before_filter :verify_authenticity_token, only: [:create]`), this endpoint can be probed without a valid token and used as an oracle to enumerate which emails are blocked/blacklisted or already registered, and reflects attacker-controlled input back. Consider not echoing the submitted values (the client already knows what it submitted).
